lesson.title: Clocking a Chemical Reaction: What We Mean by Reaction Rate
lesson.summary: Reaction rate measures how quickly reactant concentration falls or product concentration rises over time, expressed in units of concentration per time, and it is a completely separate question from whether a reaction is thermodynamically favorable in the first place.
lesson.body:
A chemical change converts reactants into products, and tracking that change quantitatively requires the same careful measurement habits used everywhere else in chemistry, here applied to concentration and time. But knowing that a reaction happens is different from knowing how fast it happens. The driving force chapter earlier in this unit established that a thermodynamically favorable reaction tends to proceed toward products, but favorability alone says nothing about speed. Diamond converting to graphite, for instance, is thermodynamically favorable at room temperature, yet it proceeds so slowly that diamonds are, for all practical purposes, forever. Reaction rate is the quantity chemists use to describe exactly this: how much the concentration of a reactant or product changes per unit of time, typically expressed in units like moles per liter per second, M/s, or moles per liter per minute, M/min.

Measuring a reaction rate in practice means tracking the concentration of one substance in the reaction as a function of time, often recorded as a table or plotted as a concentration-versus-time graph. The average rate over some time interval is simply the change in concentration divided by the change in time across that interval. The instantaneous rate at any single moment is the slope of the tangent line to the concentration-versus-time curve at that point, a more precise but conceptually identical idea.

Here is a worked example. For a general reaction A to B, a student measures [A] equal to 1.000 M at t = 0 s, and [A] equal to 0.750 M at t = 20.0 s. What is the average rate of the reaction over this interval? The change in concentration is Delta[A] = 0.750 M minus 1.000 M, which equals negative 0.250 M, a decrease, as expected since A is being consumed. The change in time is Delta t = 20.0 s minus 0 s, which equals 20.0 s. The average rate is defined as negative Delta[A] divided by Delta t, so negative (negative 0.250 M) divided by 20.0 s equals positive 0.0125 M/s.

That negative sign in front of the definition exists specifically to flip a naturally negative quantity, since a reactant's concentration is falling, into the positive number that matches the everyday intuition that a fast reaction has a large rate. This exact convention gets a formal name and a closer look in the next chapter, rate of disappearance. Reaction rate is also generally not constant over the whole course of a reaction. It tends to be fastest at the very start, when reactant concentrations are highest, and slows as reactants get used up, which is why chemists usually specify the time interval, or take the instantaneous slope at a particular moment, rather than quoting a single rate for an entire reaction. The next two chapters build on this foundation from two complementary directions: rate of disappearance, describing the rate from a reactant's point of view, and rate of appearance, describing it from a product's point of view.
